samples.scenario: Prediction target period: from 2023-10-29 to 2024-01-14. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The Biden administration announced its goal to admit up to 125,000 refugees for resettlement in the United States during the fiscal year beginning October 1, 2023. This decision was officially commended by the UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, which highlighted it as a significant step in providing safe and legal pathways for forcibly displaced individuals around the world. <2> On August 10, 2023, the Biden administration submitted a supplemental spending request to Congress that included $4 billion for border security and migration management as part of a larger $40 billion package. This funding was intended to address the humanitarian and security situation at the U.S. Southwest border. The specific allocations within the border-related funds included $2.2 billion for shelter and services for migrants released from DHS custody, nearly $800 million for initiatives to counter the trafficking of fentanyl, and $59 million for immigration judges and other needs of the immigration courts. <3> The Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), a division of the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), announced the Support for Trauma-Affected Refugees (STAR) Program for Fiscal Year 2023. This new grant program is designed to fund organizations that provide comprehensive, integrated services to refugees and other eligible newcomers who have experienced trauma that hinders their ability to function effectively. The program's goals are to improve the physical, social, emotional, and economic well-being of trauma-affected individuals and to increase their access to culturally and linguistically appropriate care. Funded services will include case management, as well as health, psychological, and social adjustment support. The program aims to foster a network of culturally responsive providers capable of addressing the psychosocial needs of these populations to facilitate their successful integration. <4> On June 23, 2023, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 8-1 in the case of United States v. Texas, allowing the Biden administration to continue its immigration enforcement policy. The Court determined that Texas and Louisiana lacked the necessary Article III legal standing to challenge the federal government's guidelines. The challenged policy, outlined in a September 2021 Department of Homeland Security memo, directs enforcement agencies to prioritize the apprehension and deportation of non-citizens who pose a threat to national security, public safety, or border security. This includes individuals suspected of terrorism, those who have committed serious crimes, and those recently apprehended at the border. The ruling affirmed the executive branch's authority to set its own enforcement priorities and exercise prosecutorial discretion. <5> The Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) issued Policy Letter (PL) 23-04, titled 'Expanding Income Disregards for RCA,' which provides guidance to states on expanding income disregards for the Refugee Cash Assistance (RCA) program. [2] The policy aims to ensure that cash grants refugees receive from various federal resettlement initiatives, similar to the Reception and Placement (R&P) program, are disregarded when determining RCA eligibility. [2] This allows refugees to maximize short-term financial assistance, better positioning them for economic self-sufficiency and community integration. [2] The guidance clarifies that states must disregard cash grants from programs equivalent to R&P and encourages them to do the same for grants from other federal resettlement initiatives. [2] The policy was implemented by various states, with guidance taking effect as of June 2023. [4, 6] <6> On June 6, 2023, the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) issued Policy Letter (PL) 23-03, authorizing the use of Afghan Supplemental Appropriations (ASA) funding for extended case management and extended community orientation services for certain Afghan arrivals. [2, 3] This policy is referenced in subsequent Dear Colleague Letters regarding the allocation of FY 2023 ASA funds, confirming its role in directing resources for these specific support services. [6] <7> The Biden administration finalized a new rule titled the 'Circumvention of Lawful Pathways,' which presumes most migrants are ineligible for asylum if they arrive at the U.S. southern land or coastal borders after traveling through another country without first seeking protection there. Under the rule, this presumption of ineligibility can be overcome through limited exceptions, such as using the CBP One app to present at a port of entry at a pre-scheduled time, having been denied asylum in a country they transited, or utilizing other existing lawful pathways. The rule, issued by the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice, took effect at 11:59 p.m. EST on May 11, 2023, immediately following the expiration of the Title 42 public health order. <8> On April 27, 2023, the U.S. Departments of State and Homeland Security jointly announced a series of significant new measures aimed at managing regional migration across the Western Hemisphere. [13] The actions are intended to curtail unlawful migration by expanding lawful pathways for protection and ensuring the safe, orderly, and humane processing of migrants. A central element of this announcement is the creation of new family reunification parole processes for individuals from El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Colombia. [9] Additionally, the United States made a commitment to significantly increase the number of refugees accepted from the Western Hemisphere, with the stated goal of doubling the number previously pledged as part of the Los Angeles Declaration on Migration and Protection. <9> On April 7, 2023, the National Immigration Forum released a legislative bulletin detailing U.S. refugee resettlement for fiscal year 2023. The report covered the first six months of the fiscal year, ending March 31, 2023, during which 18,429 refugees were resettled. Based on this rate, the Forum projected that approximately 36,858 refugees would be resettled for the entire fiscal year. This projection fell significantly short of the 125,000 refugee admissions ceiling set by the Biden administration. By the end of the fiscal year, the U.S. had actually resettled 60,014 refugees, exceeding the early projection but still less than half of the administration's goal. [1, 4, 5]

metadata.original_text: This time series records refugee support data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2023-12-24 to 2024-03-10. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The Biden administration issued a Presidential Determination on refugee admissions for Fiscal Year 2024, formally establishing regional allocations. As part of this determination, a significant number of admission spots, set between 35,000 and 50,000, were reserved for individuals from Latin America and the Caribbean. This allocation represents a key component of the administration's broader strategy for managing migration in the Western Hemisphere. <2> On September 29, 2023, President Biden signed the Presidential Determination on Refugee Admissions for Fiscal Year 2024, maintaining the ambitious goal of resettling up to 125,000 refugees. [1, 5, 8] This decision, made after consultations with Congress and justified by humanitarian concerns and the national interest, was formally published in the Federal Register on October 25, 2023. [7] The determination outlined regional allocations, providing flexibility to transfer unused slots between regions as needed to respond to global crises. [7, 8] This goal continues the Biden-Harris Administration's efforts to rebuild and strengthen the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program (USRAP) following historic lows, with a particular focus on expanding processing in the Western Hemisphere. [2, 5] <3> On September 29, 2023, the Biden administration signed the Presidential Determination on Refugee Admissions for Fiscal Year 2024, maintaining the overall admissions ceiling at 125,000 refugees. A significant shift in this directive was the increased focus on Latin America and the Caribbean, with a new target to resettle 35,000 to 50,000 refugees from this region. This represented a substantial increase from the previous fiscal year's goal of 15,000 for the region. The determination also specified that, for FY 2024, individuals in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras could be considered for refugee status. The measure was part of a broader strategy to expand legal pathways for protection in the Western Hemisphere. The official publication of this determination occurred on October 25, 2023. <4> The Biden administration announced its goal to admit up to 125,000 refugees for resettlement in the United States during the fiscal year beginning October 1, 2023. This decision was officially commended by the UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, which highlighted it as a significant step in providing safe and legal pathways for forcibly displaced individuals around the world. <5> On August 10, 2023, the Biden administration submitted a supplemental spending request to Congress that included $4 billion for border security and migration management as part of a larger $40 billion package. This funding was intended to address the humanitarian and security situation at the U.S. Southwest border. The specific allocations within the border-related funds included $2.2 billion for shelter and services for migrants released from DHS custody, nearly $800 million for initiatives to counter the trafficking of fentanyl, and $59 million for immigration judges and other needs of the immigration courts. <6> The Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), a division of the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), announced the Support for Trauma-Affected Refugees (STAR) Program for Fiscal Year 2023. This new grant program is designed to fund organizations that provide comprehensive, integrated services to refugees and other eligible newcomers who have experienced trauma that hinders their ability to function effectively. The program's goals are to improve the physical, social, emotional, and economic well-being of trauma-affected individuals and to increase their access to culturally and linguistically appropriate care. Funded services will include case management, as well as health, psychological, and social adjustment support. The program aims to foster a network of culturally responsive providers capable of addressing the psychosocial needs of these populations to facilitate their successful integration. <7> On June 23, 2023, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 8-1 in the case of United States v. Texas, allowing the Biden administration to continue its immigration enforcement policy. The Court determined that Texas and Louisiana lacked the necessary Article III legal standing to challenge the federal government's guidelines. The challenged policy, outlined in a September 2021 Department of Homeland Security memo, directs enforcement agencies to prioritize the apprehension and deportation of non-citizens who pose a threat to national security, public safety, or border security. This includes individuals suspected of terrorism, those who have committed serious crimes, and those recently apprehended at the border. The ruling affirmed the executive branch's authority to set its own enforcement priorities and exercise prosecutorial discretion. <8> The Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) issued Policy Letter (PL) 23-04, titled 'Expanding Income Disregards for RCA,' which provides guidance to states on expanding income disregards for the Refugee Cash Assistance (RCA) program. [2] The policy aims to ensure that cash grants refugees receive from various federal resettlement initiatives, similar to the Reception and Placement (R&P) program, are disregarded when determining RCA eligibility. [2] This allows refugees to maximize short-term financial assistance, better positioning them for economic self-sufficiency and community integration. [2] The guidance clarifies that states must disregard cash grants from programs equivalent to R&P and encourages them to do the same for grants from other federal resettlement initiatives. [2] The policy was implemented by various states, with guidance taking effect as of June 2023. [4, 6] <9> On June 6, 2023, the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) issued Policy Letter (PL) 23-03, authorizing the use of Afghan Supplemental Appropriations (ASA) funding for extended case management and extended community orientation services for certain Afghan arrivals. [2, 3] This policy is referenced in subsequent Dear Colleague Letters regarding the allocation of FY 2023 ASA funds, confirming its role in directing resources for these specific support services. [6]

[2, 3, 4, 6] However, the government effectively halted the program earlier, canceling refugee travel and stopping all case processing on January 21, 2025. [5] The order requires the Secretary of Homeland Security, in consultation with the Secretary of State, to report to the President every 90 days on whether resuming the program is in the national interest. [4] For example, states like Georgia, Massachusetts, and Washington put forward bills designed to reinforce the right to public education for all children, regardless of immigration status. Key activities include live storytelling events like 'The Immigrant Story Live' and resource fairs, such as the Beaverton Welcoming Week Resource Fair featuring the Pacific Refugee Support Group (PRSG), all aiming to affirm that communities are stronger when everyone feels they belong. <2> On September 9, 2025, the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI) announced its alarm over the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) decision to terminate the 2021 Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation for Venezuela. Noem, temporarily blocking the Department of Homeland Security from applying expedited removal procedures to individuals who previously entered the U.S. on humanitarian parole. [2] According to the Council, these actions represent a wholesale effort to use the immigration system to undermine democratic principles and exercise unchecked executive power. [2] The report warns that these policies are reshaping the immigration system in ways that are unfair, unlawful, and inconsistent with American values. [2] <7> A hearing in the case of CHIRLA v. Noem was held on July 9, 2025, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia before Judge Jia M. Cobb. Noem, challenges the termination of these parole programs and the subsequent halt in processing immigration applications for those who entered under these and other programs like Uniting for Ukraine (U4U) and family reunification parole. The updated policy applies to applications pending or filed on or after December 5, 2025. <5> On November 21, 2025, USCIS Director Joe Edlow issued an internal memo ordering the review of over 200,000 lawfully admitted refugees who entered the United States between January 21, 2021, and February 20, 2025. Kennedy, Jr. and Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) Interim Director Angie Salazar. The letter strongly condemned recent actions by the Trump administration, demanding answers regarding policies that have significantly extended detention periods, placed children in harm's way, and jeopardized the overall safety of unaccompanied children in federal custody. <8> The Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), under the Department of Health and Human Services, notified legal service providers about a new Department of Homeland Security (DHS) initiative targeting unaccompanied migrant children. Under this program, DHS is offering a one-time $2,500 'resettlement support stipend' to unaccompanied minors aged 14 and older currently in ORR custody. The financial incentive is provided in exchange for the children electing voluntary departure from the United States, an option that requires them to waive their rights to a hearing before an immigration judge. <9> A federal government shutdown commenced, causing a delay in the official Federal Register publication of the Fiscal Year 2026 refugee admissions determination. By law, the President is required to set the annual refugee ceiling before the start of the fiscal year on October 1. Consequently, the shutdown threatened the disruption of Refugee Cash Assistance (RCA) and other federal programs tied to this timeline. <10> On September 30, 2025, Presidential Determination No. 2025-14 was signed to transfer the administration of the United States Program of Initial Refugee Resettlement from the Department of State to the Department of Health and Human Services' Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR). The determination was subsequently published in the Federal Register on October 31, 2025, centralizing domestic resettlement responsibilities under one agency.
